canonical.reference_answer: The surgeon performs a continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC): after an initial nick in the anterior capsule with a cystotome or forceps, the tear is extended circumferentially in small controlled bites, regrasping close to the tear edge each time, aiming for a round, centered capsulorhexis roughly 5.0-5.5mm in diameter. Adequate anterior chamber depth (viscoelastic) and consistent, low, tangential tearing force are the key technical requirements; radial extension (a tear that runs outward toward the equator instead of curving back) is the primary failure mode to watch for.
known_pitfalls: Radial 'runaway' extension toward the capsular equator
Small or off-center capsulorhexis restricting later steps
Loss of red reflex / poor visualization leading to tear tracking errors
Chamber shallowing mid-tear from viscoelastic dissipation

canonical.reference_answer: The surgeon sculpts and divides the lens nucleus (e.g. divide-and-conquer or chop technique) using ultrasound energy delivered through the phaco probe, then emulsifies and aspirates the fragments while a second instrument stabilizes/manipulates the nucleus. Key technical requirements: staying centered in the capsular bag and away from the posterior capsule and corneal endothelium, maintaining chamber stability, and using the minimum effective ultrasound energy/time. Common pitfalls include posterior capsule rupture from probe depth misjudgment, chasing mobile fragments outside the safe zone, and endothelial trauma from probe proximity to the cornea.
